families.title: Tile gardens: missing square
families.mathematics: An a by b rectangle (a < b) and the square whose side is the average of its sides, m = (a + b)/2. Cut the rectangle into an m by a piece and an a by (b − a)/2 piece: the first lies across the square and leaves a band (b − a)/2 tall, which the second fills except one square of side (b − a)/2. So m² = ab + ((b − a)/2)²: the average-side square always has more area than the rectangle, by exactly that square. Shortening the square’s other side to ab/m keeps the area: that is Week 93’s reshaping move, which narrows the side of the equal-area square between ab/m and m every time and never reaches it (Newton’s method for a square root). With one straight cut the only solve cuts m off the long side, and the square left over sits in a corner; other places need more pieces, and squares that pairwise can’t share a rectangular piece prove how many.
rules: Cut only along the grid lines, straight across a piece, at most once. The scissors show the cuts left.
Every piece goes in the square, on the grid, with no overlaps; pieces may be turned.
Solved when the part left uncovered is one square.

puzzles.idea: The square’s side, 3, is the average of 4 and 2. Cut 3 off the long side: the 3 by 2 lies across the square and the turned 2 by 1 leaves a 1 by 1 square, half of 4 − 2.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: cutting, dragging and turning are taps. Counting squares to about 10; halving and taking away explain the size of the square left over.
hints: Which piece could lie right across the square?
A piece as long as the square is wide fits across it.
Cut the 4 by 2 into a 3 by 2 and a 2 by 1, then turn the small piece.

parent.notice: Whether your child cuts in the middle first, and sees why two 2 by 2 pieces can’t both fit in a 3 by 3 square.
parent.prompt: Why does the square’s side, 3, suit this rectangle so well?
parent.explanation: 3 is halfway between 2 and 4. Cut 3 off the long side: the 3 by 2 piece lies across the square and leaves a 3 by 1 row, and the 2 by 1 piece, turned, covers two of its squares and leaves one. The areas agree: 9 − 8 = 1. Cutting in the middle fails, because two 2 by 2 pieces in a 3 by 3 square would both need its middle square.
parent.extension: What would be left uncovered from a 6 by 2 in a 4 by 4 square? (Puzzle 2.)
parent.connection: The square whose side is the average of a rectangle’s sides holds the rectangle with one square left over, of side half the difference.

puzzles.provenance: Week 93 Problem 2, rectangle B (4 by 2 into a 3 by 3 square), with a one-cut limit added.

puzzles.idea: Cut 4 off the 6: the 4 by 2 lies across the square and the 2 by 2 fills half the band above, leaving a 2 by 2 square in a corner.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: cutting, dragging and turning are taps. Counting squares to about 10; halving and taking away explain the size of the square left over.
hints: Which piece could lie right across the square?
Cut a piece as long as the square is wide.
Cut the 6 by 2 into a 4 by 2 and a 2 by 2.

parent.notice: Whether your child cuts at 3 first (two 3 by 2 pieces), and finds that those never leave a single square.
parent.prompt: How big is the square left over, and where can it be?
parent.explanation: The 4 by 2 lies across the 4 by 4 square and leaves a 4 by 2 band; the 2 by 2 sits at one end and leaves a 2 by 2 square in a corner, and 16 − 12 = 4. With one cut, the cut is always 2 from an end (a 4 by 2 and a 2 by 2) and the uncovered square is always in a corner; two 3 by 2 pieces never leave one square.
parent.extension: Leave the uncovered square in the middle of the top edge instead. How many cuts does that take? (Two: puzzle 9.)
parent.connection: Week 93’s identity m² − ab = ((b − a)/2)², here 16 − 12 = 2 × 2.

puzzles.idea: The uncovered square has side 2, half of 5 − 1. Puzzles 1 and 2 also fit “half the long side, minus 1”; this one tells the two rules apart.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start: cutting, dragging and turning are taps. Counting squares to about 10; halving and taking away explain the size of the square left over.
hints: Which piece could lie across the bottom of the square?
A 3 by 1 lies across. Where can the rest go?
Cut it into a 3 by 1 and a 2 by 1, and stand the 2 by 1 up in a corner.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts the uncovered square from puzzles 1 and 2 before fitting.
parent.prompt: Puzzles 1 and 2 both had short side 2. What rule fits all three?
parent.explanation: The 3 by 1 lies across the bottom; the 2 by 1, stood up in a corner, leaves a 2 by 2 square, and 9 − 5 = 4. In puzzles 1 and 2 the uncovered side is also half the long side minus 1, but here that would be 1½. The rule that fits all three is half the difference of the sides: (5 − 1) ÷ 2 = 2.
parent.extension: Predict the square left over when 9 by 1 goes into 5 by 5. (Side 4.)
parent.connection: The Week 93 review card added this case (its fix 1) to separate the two rules.

puzzles.idea: One cut along a line from the missing corner, and the pieces make the 4 by 2 again. No other rectangle comes from one cut.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start. Counting squares, and rows times columns for area, help to see which rectangles are possible.
hints: Cut along a line that starts at the missing corner.
Put the two pieces end to end.
Cut off the 2 by 1 at the top and put it at the end of the 3 by 2.

parent.notice: Whether your child looks for a second rectangle before pressing That’s all, and how they decide there isn’t one.
parent.prompt: Could the 8 squares make an 8 by 1 with one cut?
parent.explanation: Cutting along either line from the missing corner gives a 3 by 2 and a 2 by 1, which make a 4 by 2: the square with its corner gone is the 4 by 2, rearranged. Eight squares make only 8 by 1 and 4 by 2, and an 8 by 1 needs every piece one square thick, which one cut can’t give.
parent.extension: With two cuts, the shape can make an 8 by 1.
parent.connection: This is puzzle 1 run backwards: the 4 by 2 becomes the 3 by 3 square with a 1 by 1 corner gone, and back again.

puzzles.provenance: New: the reverse move from the review card’s App fit, on the shape Problem 2’s rectangle B leaves.

parent.prompt: Before fitting: how big will the square left over be?
parent.explanation: The 5 by 2 lies across the square and leaves a 5 by 3 band; the 3 by 2, turned, covers two columns of it and leaves a 3 by 3 square. 25 − 16 = 9.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects the same square left over as in puzzle 5, since the square is the same.
parent.prompt: Puzzles 5 and 6 both fill a 5 by 5 square. Why are the squares left over different?
parent.explanation: The 5 by 3 lies across the square and leaves a 5 by 2 band; the 3 by 2, turned, covers three of its columns and leaves a 2 by 2 square. 25 − 21 = 4. The square’s side is the average, 5, for both 8 by 2 and 7 by 3; the side left over is half the difference, 3 for 8 by 2 and 2 for 7 by 3. A rectangle nearer to a square leaves a smaller square over.
parent.extension: Which rectangle with sides adding to 10 leaves the smallest square over? (6 by 4 leaves a 1 by 1.)
parent.connection: Week 93 Problem 6: the extra area is ((b − a)/2)², so the closer the sides, the smaller the square left over.

puzzles.idea: Two rectangles: the 6 by 2 it came from, and a 4 by 3, whose side 4 is the average of 6 and 2 and whose other side is 12 ÷ 4. That is Week 93’s reshaping move.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start. Counting squares, and rows times columns for area, help to see which rectangles are possible.
hints: Make the rectangle it came from first.
Is there another? Try cutting off a thinner strip.
Cut off the 2 by 1 at the top and fit it into the notch.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps looking after the 6 by 2, and sees that the 4 by 3 needs a different cut.
parent.prompt: How are 6 by 2 and 4 by 3 related?
parent.explanation: Cutting along a line from the missing corner gives a 4 by 2 and a 2 by 2, which make the 6 by 2. Cutting off the top row gives a 2 by 1 that fills the notch of what is left: a 4 by 3. That is Week 93’s reshaping move: from 6 by 2, take the average side, (6 + 2) ÷ 2 = 4, and divide the area by it, 12 ÷ 4 = 3. No other rectangle comes from one cut; 12 by 1 would need every piece one square thick.
parent.extension: Reshape 4 by 3 the same way: the average is 3½ and the other side 12 ÷ 3½ = 24/7. The sides are no longer whole squares, and it is still not a square.
parent.connection: Repeating the reshaping move is Newton’s method for a square root: the sides close in on the side of the square of area 12 from both ends and never reach it.

puzzles.provenance: New: the review card’s reverse move (“which 12-tile rectangle reshapes to 3 by 4?”), played on the shape Problem 2’s rectangle A leaves.

parent.prompt: What will be left uncovered, and why?

puzzles.objective: Cut the rectangle (2 cuts at most) and fit every piece in the square around the dashed square, or press Can’t and tap squares that each need a piece of their own, more than the cuts can make.

Every piece goes in the square, on the grid, with no overlaps; pieces may be turned. The dashed square stays uncovered.

Can’t: tap squares no one piece could cover two of, more of them than the cuts make pieces. A piece is a rectangle, so two squares can share one only when the rectangle between them misses the dashed square.
puzzles.idea: The dashed square in the middle of the top edge leaves a post on each side and a base below: three pieces, a 4 by 2 base and the 2 by 2 cut into two 2 by 1 posts.
puzzles.prerequisites: The earlier Missing square puzzles. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: What shapes are the spaces round the dashed square?
The base is a 4 by 2. What fills each side of the dashed square?
Cut the 6 by 2 into a 4 by 2 and a 2 by 2, then cut the 2 by 2 in half.

parent.notice: Whether your child plans the pieces from the space to fill, rather than cutting first.
parent.prompt: Why can’t two pieces do it?
parent.explanation: The top-left square, the top-right square and the square under the dashed one can’t share pieces: every piece is a rectangle, and a rectangle holding two of them covers part of the dashed square. So three pieces are needed, and two cuts make three: a 4 by 2 base and two 2 by 1 posts. With one cut the square left over is always in a corner.
parent.extension: Can the dashed square be in the very middle with two cuts? (Puzzle 10.)
parent.connection: Squares that pairwise can’t share a piece give a lower bound on the number of pieces; Can’t asks for such squares.

puzzles.provenance: New: the review card’s harder goal, naming the uncovered square’s place within a piece budget.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries several cuttings before suspecting it can’t be done, and how they explain it.
parent.prompt: Why can’t one piece touch two sides of the dashed square?
parent.explanation: Every piece is a rectangle. A rectangle holding squares beside two different sides of the dashed square would cover part of it. So the four squares beside its sides (the middle one beside each side, say) need four different pieces, and two cuts make only three. With three cuts it works (puzzle 11).
parent.extension: With three cuts, which four pieces go round it?
parent.connection: Squares no two of which can share a piece are a certificate: anyone can check it, pair by pair, without trying every cutting.

puzzles.idea: Four 5 by 2 pieces wind round the dashed square like a pinwheel: cut the 10 by 4 into two 10 by 2 strips and cut each in half.
puzzles.prerequisites: The earlier Missing square puzzles. Reading the Can’t rule with a grown-up the first time.
hints: Each side of the dashed square needs its own piece. How big could the four pieces be?
Four equal pieces can go round it like a pinwheel.
Cut the 10 by 4 into two 10 by 2 pieces, then cut each into two 5 by 2 pieces.

parent.notice: Whether your child uses puzzle 10’s reason to plan four pieces.
parent.prompt: Why do four pieces of one size fit?
parent.explanation: The space round the dashed square is a frame 2 squares wide. Four 5 by 2 pieces, each along one side and reaching one corner, fill it like a pinwheel: 4 × 10 = 40 = 49 − 9. From the 10 by 4: halve it into two 10 by 2 strips, then cut each strip in half, three cuts. Two 7 by 2 and two 3 by 2 pieces (strips cut at 7) fill it too.
parent.extension: Fill the frame with two 7 by 2 and two 3 by 2 pieces.
parent.connection: Puzzle 10’s four squares show that four pieces are needed; here four are enough.

puzzles.title: Three by three gone
puzzles.objective: Cut the shape (2 cuts at most) and make every rectangle you can from all of its pieces, then press That’s all.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Make every rectangle you can from all the pieces.
puzzles.instruction: Cut the shape (2 cuts at most) and make every rectangle you can from all of its pieces, then press That’s all.
puzzles.controls: Pieces are cut at the top, before they go on the grid. Tap a piece there to choose it: dashed lines cross it where it can be cut, and a tap on a line cuts there. Drag a piece onto the grid below, or tap the grid where its top-left corner goes; it turns if it fits only turned. Tap a chosen piece again, or press Turn, to turn it; from the top it comes onto the grid turned. Drag a piece back up, or tap its empty place, to take it back. Tape joins every piece back together. Every rectangle made goes on the shelf below; press That’s all when you think every one is there.
rules: Cut only along the grid lines, straight across a piece, at most 2 times. The scissors show the cuts left.
A rectangle uses every piece, side to side, with no gaps or overlaps. A rectangle turned round is the same one.
That’s all says every rectangle the pieces can make is on the shelf.
puzzles.idea: With two cuts the shape makes the 8 by 2 it came from, and also a 4 by 4 square: 16 squares is 4 by 4.
puzzles.prerequisites: None to start. Counting squares, and rows times columns for area, help to see which rectangles are possible.
hints: Make the rectangle it came from first.
Sixteen squares could make a square. How long is its side?
Cut off the 2 by 1 at the top, then cut a 3 by 2 off the bottom right. The three pieces make a 4 by 4.

parent.notice: Whether your child looks for a square once the 8 by 2 is found, and connects 16 with 4 by 4.
parent.prompt: The reshaping move never makes a square. How did cutting make one?
parent.explanation: One cut along a line from the missing corner gives a 3 by 2 and a 5 by 2, which make the 8 by 2. Two cuts can give a 2 by 1, a 4 by 2 and a 3 by 2, which make a 4 by 4, since 16 is a square number. The reshaping move (8 by 2, then 5 by 16/5, …) always keeps one side the average and closes in on 4 without reaching it; cutting freely reaches a square whenever the area is a square number. No other rectangle comes from two cuts.
parent.extension: Which rectangles can the 4 by 4 with a 2 by 2 corner gone make with two cuts? (Still only 6 by 2 and 4 by 3.)
parent.connection: Any two shapes of the same area made of squares can be cut into each other (into single squares, if nothing else); the question is how few cuts are enough.

puzzles.provenance: New: the review card’s reverse move with two cuts, on the shape the 8 by 2 of puzzle 5 leaves.
